content: 1. An appropriate approach for couple and partner testing should include supportive options such as provider assistance. However, there are specific situations where couple or partner testing may not be advisable. 2. Strategies to improve access to HIV testing services include task-sharing. Lay providers who are adequately trained and supervised can independently perform safe and effective HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests. This is strongly recommended based on moderate-certainty evidence. 3. To maintain the accuracy and reliability of HIV diagnosis, Western blotting and line immunoassays should not be used in national HIV testing strategies and algorithms. This is a strong recommendation supported by low-certainty evidence. 4. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all HIV testing algorithms achieve at least 99% positive predictive value and utilize a combination of tests with ≥99% sensitivity and ≥98% specificity. The first test in an HIV testing strategy should have the highest sensitivity, followed by second and third tests with the highest specificity. 5. Countries should consider adopting a three-test strategy when the HIV positivity rate in national testing programs falls below 5%. This means individuals should have three consecutive reactive test results to confirm an HIV-positive diagnosis. 6. Dual HIV/syphilis rapid diagnostic tests can be used as the first test in HIV testing strategies for antenatal care. 7. WHO suggests using a testing strategy suitable for both HIV diagnosis during surveillance and for routinely returning HIV test results to participants. 8. All individuals newly diagnosed with HIV should be retested to confirm their HIV status before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART), using the same testing strategy and algorithm as the initial diagnosis. 9. Retesting individuals who already know their HIV-positive status, including those on ART, is not recommended as it may yield incorrect results due to ART's effects. 10. Adding nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth to existing early infant diagnosis approaches can be considered to identify HIV infection in HIV-exposed infants. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 11. Point-of-care nucleic acid testing is strongly recommended for diagnosing HIV in infants and children younger than 18 months, supported by high-certainty evidence. 12. Rapid diagnostic tests for HIV serology can be used to assess HIV exposure in infants younger than four months. For infants aged four to 18 months, HIV exposure status should be determined by testing the mother. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 13. Rapid diagnostic tests for HIV serology can also be used to diagnose HIV infection in children older than 18 months, following national testing strategies. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 14. To minimize false-positive results in infant diagnosis using NAT, an indeterminate range of viral copy equivalents should be introduced to improve accuracy. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 15. The correct and consistent use of condoms with compatible lubricants is strongly recommended for all key populations to prevent sexual transmission of HIV and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). This is supported by moderate-certainty evidence. 16. Individuals from key populations who inject drugs should have access to sterile injecting equipment through needle and syringe programs. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 17. People dependent on opioids should be offered opioid substitution therapy in line with WHO guidance, including those in prison or other closed settings. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 18. Key populations with harmful alcohol or substance use should have access to evidence-based interventions, including brief psychosocial interventions involving assessment, specific feedback, and advice. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 19. People likely to witness an opioid overdose should have access to naloxone and be trained in its use for emergency management of suspected opioid overdose. This is a strong recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 20. Voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) should continue to be promoted as an effective HIV prevention option for adolescent boys aged 15 years and older and adult men in settings with generalized epidemics. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence. 21. WHO-prequalified male circumcision devices are recommended as additional methods for male circumcision in the context of HIV prevention for males aged 15 years and older. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 22. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) should be offered as an additional prevention choice for individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection as part of combination prevention approaches. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence. 23. The dapivirine vaginal ring may be offered as an additional prevention choice for cisgender women at substantial risk of HIV infection as part of combination prevention approaches. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 24. HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) regimens with two antiretroviral (ARV) drugs are effective, but three-drug regimens are preferred. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 25. For adults and adolescents, TDF + 3TC (or FTC) is the preferred backbone regimen for HIV PEP. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 26. Dolutegravir (DTG) is recommended as the preferred third drug for HIV PEP. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 27. Alternative third-drug options for PEP, such as ATV/r, DRV/r, LPV/r, and RAL, may be considered when available. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 28. For children aged 10 years and younger, AZT + 3TC is the preferred backbone regimen for HIV PEP. ABC + 3TC or TDF + 3TC (or FTC) may be considered as alternatives. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 29. DTG is recommended as the preferred third drug for HIV PEP in children with approved DTG dosing. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 30. Infants born to mothers with HIV who are at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with daily AZT and NVP for the first six weeks of life, regardless of feeding method. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 31. Breastfed infants at high risk of acquiring HIV should continue infant prophylaxis for an additional six weeks (total of 12 weeks) using either AZT and NVP or NVP alone. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 32. ART should be initiated for all people living with HIV regardless of WHO clinical stage or CD4 cell count. Rapid ART initiation should be offered to all individuals following a confirmed HIV diagnosis and clinical assessment. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents and low-certainty evidence for children. 33. ART initiation should be offered on the same day to individuals ready to start. This is a strong recommendation with high-certainty evidence for adults and adolescents and low-certainty evidence for children. 34. Immediate ART initiation is not recommended for individuals with cryptococcal meningitis due to the risk of increased mortality. ART should be deferred by 4–6 weeks from the initiation of antifungal treatment. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence for adults and very low-certainty evidence for children and adolescents. 35. ART should be initiated as soon as possible for individuals with disseminated histoplasmosis without central nervous system involvement. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 36. Viral load testing is recommended as the preferred monitoring approach to diagnose and confirm treatment failure. Plasma specimens are preferred for viral load testing, but dried blood spot specimens are recommended in settings where logistical or operational barriers prevent routine plasma testing. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence.
